utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Wednesday, May 13th, 2009, and I would like to welcome Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Stojic. I also greet Mr. Praljak this morning, and I of course would not forget our counsels, Mr. Stringer and all his associates, as well as the people helping us. I'd like to tell Mr. Kovacic that up until now he has used up 12 hours, and that's one-third of the time allocated for Mr. Praljak's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I have two follow-up questions that I thought about during the night, and it's important for me I believe to think about it. The first one, you told us yesterday, as regards Mr. Tudjman's speech before the Croatian officers, if I'm not mistaken, I believe that your case is that the officers in the Croatian Army - and I'm talking about the Croatian Army now, not the HVO - I think that your case is that these were officers who had joined the Croatian Army without any political commitment whatsoever. And as an officer in the Croatian Army, you were not supposed to talk about your political opinions. We know, because you told us that; we know that you were the general secretary of a small political party for a while. But this is my question: When you actually joined the Croatian Army, did you put aside your political opinions that you may have had at the time, and in the framework of your military career and mission you were only executing the orders received from Tudjman through the Ministry of Defence, without taking your political opinions into consideration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. That's not how it was in its entirety. A good part of the officers and some of the key persons were listed yesterday who had come in from the ranks of the JNA, joined because of their political judgement, but now I would like to draw a distinction between politics in a well-ordered state, where you deal with taxes and things like that. I always refer to this as a pre-political era. It's actually morality as politics. So these people came in for political reasons, so to speak, because they no longer wanted to be in the ranks of the Yugoslav People’s army that began serving the interests of a policy advocating Greater Serbia. So this is,conditionally speaking, political conviction, although I would like to use a different term for that. I was a secretary general of a party that was not really all that small. It was the third-largest party in Croatia. And again, as all the other parties at the time, we're not talking about politics as the term is understood today. All the statutes and all the platforms of all the parties in Croatia were alike, like peas in a pod. They all wanted a peaceful solution to the Yugoslav crisis. They all advocated democracy, free elections, a free market economy. So these are the basic tenets which at one point, once the state is in place, would make political life possible. And in this sense, when I was involved in politics before, this had nothing to do, and my desire to get involved in politics, when you use the term "politics," what you mean, when you use the term. Thirdly, a large number of people who joined the Croatian Army joined for political reasons, conditionally speaking, but we're not again talking about politics in the usual sense of the term. It was their moral obligation to defend yourself if you're under attack, the moral obligation. If politics is actually striving for democracy, for free-market economy, then, yes, it's politics. However, in the Croatian Army, political debates were banned, and Croatian soldiers and officers were not allowed to attend political rallies or any other kinds of demonstrations in uniform. As soldiers, they were not allowed to be involved in politics. They were supposed to pursue the Croatian state policy, the conclusions of the Parliament, the government or the president. That's what they were supposed to follow. And then if somebody wanted to be politically active because there were elections and so on, they were free to do so, we followed the German model which says a soldier is a civilian in uniform, and once they take off their uniform, they can participate in the political life. But if they are nominated or elected to a position, they have to leave the army. And once again please bear in mind that this term "politics" should not be understood in the same way that it should as it is understood today in France, USA, and so on. It was simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this. A second question, it's a technical question, but I believe it's important. Yesterday, you showed us a number of documents dealing with Mr. Tudjman and Croatian politics, and trying to establish that as regards the JCE, Mr. Tudjman had no desire whatsoever to annex any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Very well. You showed us a number of documents to this end. Given this, I wonder the following, as far as global control is concerned. I'm sure you read all judgements rendered by this Tribunal, Blaskic, Kordic, Aleksovski and others - I'm not going to mention them all - Tadic also, but I'm sure that your counsel and yourself looked at this, looked into this. And you know that as far as Croatia and the HVO are concerned, a number of judgements were rendered already. In Blaskic, for example, the Trial Chamber recognised the existence of global control. I'm sure you also know that in the Aleksovski case, the majority of Judges did not rule on the existence of a global control of Croatia over the HVO. The Appeals Chamber denied this, however, basing itself on the interpretation of the Tadic appeals judgement. In this interpretation, global control must be assessed according to a number of parameters, and the fact that a state would supply weapons, provide training, and give money is not sufficient. The state must also play a role in the military operations conducted by an armed group or a fighting unit in the other state. Therefore, there needs to be a role played, which is not like the majority of Judges had thought in the Aleksovski case. Giving a specific instruction is not sufficient; it also needs to play a role. So my question -- you see, my questions are becoming increasingly specific, and here's my question: When you were heading the HVO from July to November - you see it's a very specific period of time, my question deals with this very specific period of time from July to November - I would like to know whether at that time, as far as you know, in the framework of the military operation that you personally led, since you were in charge of the military operations as commander of the HVO, I'd like to know whether, as far as you know, at that time you felt that, as far as your command was concerned, or maybe as far as the instructions you were obtaining from Mr. Boban, who, let me remind everyone, at the time was the commander of the HVO army, I mean he was the supreme leader of this, did you feel at the time that the Republic of Croatia actually played a role in the military operations that you led?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never, Your Honour. Not even Boban told me anything at any point. At the time when I was the commander, I think that I met with Mr. Boban only briefly on two occasions. I came when Bugojno had already fallen and when the Muslim BH army offensive had been launched, and that lasted up until the intensity was reduced a little bit by mid-October and there was this line from Uskoplje, Donji Vakuf, down to Mostar. During that time, I never saw, I never spoke, I never met with Mr. Franjo Tudjman, and I think that I saw Gojko Susak only on one occasion, I think. But I think we only saw each other. It was, I think, the 1st of August, five or six days after I had arrived, when all my lines were broken in Uskoplje, when the troops and the people started pulling out. And automatically this meant that Rama might fall and there was the threat of a general collapse, and I managed to restore the lines. I saw Gojko Susak on that occasion because he had been visiting with his mother, who lived near Siroki Brijeg. We met very briefly. I told him that we managed to restore the lines, and he never influenced in any way, he never said anything during my tenure in command. I was a commander who made military decisions, and those military decisions mostly had to do with how to defend ourselves. And this went on day by day, night by night. That's how it is in the war. I think that everybody knows that. Constant fighting on long lines. I would lose some positions. I would then recapture them. When I say "I," I mean "we." And so I never discussed that with Mate Boban. Well, I didn't have anything to discuss with him. We had to defend ourselves. I never spoke to Franjo Tudjman. And I think that I only met and spoke with Gojko Susak that day when he came to visit his mother. If you allow me, I will recount an event to show you what it was -- what it looked like. Here, near Neum [indicates] - well, it's difficult to see - Bosnia and Herzegovina has its exit onto the sea, and we had lines here from Stolac to Neum [indicates]. However, the roads here are either nonexistent or are in a very bad shape. So in order to defend this Neum area here, we had to rotate our units in such a way that we had to go to Metkovic. Well, it's very difficult to see. We had to drive them to Neum from Metkovic and then take them to their positions. And when a shift was being relieved, the Croatian police in Metkovic said, pursuant to the complaints that Croatia was taking part in that, that they would no longer let the troops of the other state pass, and they made them go back from the border. Now, I, of course, asked the military police to put the police on the BH border in Neum, and then the Croatian Army that was supposed to relieve positions in Dubrovnik came to the border, and the military police officers from the HVO said, No. Then I got a phone call, not from the military part but from Interior Minister Mr. Jaganac [phoen], and he asked me, Well, why won't you let us pass through to Dubrovnik? And I said, well, why don't you want to let us pass through Neum? We are a state, we have our own borders, and you will not pass. This tells you how complicated the relationship was. Of course, then he wanted us to make some arrangements, and then I said, Okay, I'll let you pass through Dubrovnik, because they had no other way. They had to pass through the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I also told him, You have to let my army, the army under my command, pass through the border here at Metkovic to get to Neum [indicates], because I have no other way to get to those positions, because there were no roads, and Serbs held this area here [indicates]. So I quarrelled and I argued that because Croatia was being defended here, that they should take up the defence of this part of the territory so that the Croatian Defence Council should not be defending Croatia from those positions. At one point, they agreed to it, and then we let the Croatian Army hold the positions here because it was defending Croatian territory. But the international community, and I know that it was actually the Americans, said that Croatian Army troops could not be on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so we had to pull them out. I still don't understand why I was supposed to be defending Metkovic and all the other areas, because there was nothing else to be defended there. It was no -- there was no point for those units to be defending Neum here. So it was a complex situation, a complicated border-line, and it was not the idea that it was another state intervening in this state, but it was just that the Croatian Army had to defend its positions here in the south, and that's what they had to do. At one point, they agreed, and then under American pressure, I think, they bowed to this pressure, and I think there was a UN Security Council resolution about the Croatian Army pulling back from the BH borders. I think that it had to do with this, If you don't allow me to get my troops to here through Metkovic, then I won't let you get your troops through this area here to your positions. And tensions ran really high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak -- excuse me, Mr. Kovacic. This refers exactly to what Mr. Praljak has recently said. And maybe there is an error in translation. I'm referring to page 8, line 6, and the following. It starts by you saying: "At one point they agreed to it, and then we let the Croatian Army hold the positions here, because it was defending Croatian territory." Then you speak of reactions of the international community, and the conclusion is: "So we had to pull them out," which can only refer to the Croatian troops. Now, it seems that in the first part of the paragraph, you identify with Herceg-Bosna and the HVO, and in the last part you identify with Croatia. I wonder how this is to be explained. I'm sure you have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake in using the pronouns "we," "they." It may be an interpretation, whatever. The HVO had very few soldiers, that was the point, so we, the HVO, that is, asked that this area here from Stolac [indicates] -- to the right is where we were. There's Stolac [indicates]. So we were up until this area here [indicates], and then we asked the Croatian Army defend this portion of Croatia [indicates], and to the right of Stolac, since Metkovic, which was in Croatia, was being attacked, that it should be taken over by the Croatian Army. At one point in time, they agreed to do that, and small units of the HVO, TG-2, Tactical Group 2, that is, withdrew, and the Croatian army came in to relieve them. Then there were complaints and objections, as far as I know, from the Americans that the Croatian Army was on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this was in violation of some law or convention or whatever. And then the situation returned to what it had been previously. The Croatian Army withdrew, and we once again took up this position here [indicates], in fact, defending the borders of Croatia. Now, I spoke about a misunderstanding in that respect, that once again they, that is to say, the Croatian Army, under pressure probably, at one point banned us from going through Metkovic and bringing our troops in to defend this area here around Neum [indicates], because you couldn't reach this area by any other route. Then I banned the Croatian Army from crossing over into Dubrovnik across Bosnian and Herzegovinian territory. And then there was this whole dispute, and we agreed to let them through and they would let us through, because how else could you defend that area? There were no planes. You couldn't take the sea route. So that was a classical situation and the kind of problems that cropped up. But there was a dispute over this, and as far as I know, and I think my information is very correct, although maybe not 100 percent, that the existence of this area here [indicates] caused the existence of the Croatian Army, which at one time took over this line to the right of Stolac and TG-2, led to the resolution being passed to the effect that the Croatian Army was on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although it was unable to defend its own territory of this narrow space around the south here in any other way from the mouth of the River Neretva from that whole area there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask the general to specify the time-frame of this dispute that he's described with the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Petkovic. You know dates better than me. You know, sometimes dates are a little bit fuzzy. Well, I can't know everything. There was so many events, so many events, lots and lots of them, that I might be wrong in giving a date. I don't really think dates are that important in all that general chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] well, could you start off by telling us the year? You must know the year, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What year was it? 1993, between July and November? It was between July and November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Petkovic. I don't really -- I don't know. Don't make me say it. I know the problem, I know the telephones, the conversations, the events, but everything has become mixed up. Sometimes I don't what happened from one year to the next, so why do you want me say something that I'm not sure of? I'll make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, regarding all this, you said that the Americans did not want the Croatian Army to enter into Bosnia-Herzegovina. The a few days ago, you told us that the 6th Fleet, the US 6th Fleet, was around, so I believe that through their monitoring system, they noted and they found out that the Croatian Army had actually entered into Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is why they actually stepped in or intervened. Do you agree with this, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The American officers -- well, the military attache and his assistant had an absolute right to go to any part of the territory in the theatre of war, and I took them, for example, in 1992, when they were researching into whether the factory of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bijelo Polje by Mostar could have produced noxious matter, and they were there with some experts and a Croatian Army general who used to be a general and partisan -- he was a general of the JNA who had retired and then was reactivated. Binenfeld was one of those. And then they were very interested in seeing whether or not, in that factory in Bijelo Polje - I don't know what iterate or some poisonous noxious matter could have been produced - and they took examples, and they visited me in Uskoplje, and they went wherever they wanted to, whenever they wanted to. They didn't need the US 6th Fleet. And I know that there was some carriers and something controlling the entry of ships. But they didn't need the fleet, because all the military attaches could move around Croatia however they wanted to, together with the US monitors -- UN monitors and UNPROFOR and all the rest of it, except when there was fighting going on, and then we'd tell them, Don't go, because we can't guarantee your safety. Something might happen to you, and then we'll be blamed for that. So those were the only days when -- it was only when there was fierce fighting going on that, for their own safety, we asked them not to move around. So I claim, I state, Your Honours, as somebody who granted permission, that anybody, any journalist, any European Observer or Monitor, all the military attaches could move around freely in Herzegovina and Bosnia, up to Uskoplje while they were there, whenever they wanted to and however much they wanted to, and they had all the information provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everybody -- good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, General, with respect to the first two questions that Judge Antonetti asked you, I have a follow-up question which wasn't fully clarified. To go back to Judge Antonetti's first question, you didn't expressly and specifically answer and say whether you, in formal terms, in real terms, ceased to be a member of the HDS before you joined the ministry or, rather, the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the spring of 1991, I stepped down from the Croatian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to go back to Judge Antonetti's second question. When you were discussing relations with the Croatian Army and the HVO commander - which is what you were - so while you were HVO commander from July to November, did you ever talk or meet a commander of the Main Staff of the HV, General Stipetic?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Stipetic wasn't the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I might have got the name wrong, but with the chief of the Main Staff of the HV?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Had you had any military cooperation in the field, by the very nature of your business, would you have had to have met and had contacts with the chief of the Main Staff of the HV?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been very necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps I can help out -- help Your Honours out with respect to the explanations that Mr. Praljak spoke about, the complicated situation around the border around Metkovic. The 3D03544 map that we provided you with, which was the A-3 laminated version, it's a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you look at it carefully, and I think that you already know this, there's a part over there -- a part of the coast which is the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Croatia hasn't got a continuous coastline, continuous territory along the coast, so that, for example, you could go from -- if you went from Split to Dubrovnik, taking the road -- the coastal road which is parallel to the coastline, you have to pass through several miles - I think it's nine miles or whatever - you have to pass through the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if you know this, then the situation is quite clear, the detail that the general spoke about, that at one point in time, for the Croatian Army to move towards Dubrovnik, the HVO placed itself at the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina and said, No, to the Croatian Army, you can't pass this way. You can't take this route. Well, that is just by way of explaining the map to you, if it is of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood very well. So territorially speaking, there's no continuity; Croatia is cut off at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just another explanation. Croatia wasn't cut off at that point in time. Croatia is cut off in the same way today. Bosnia-Herzegovina always had an outlet to the sea at Neum, and which means that Croatia -- there was always a gap in Croatia along that area, along that portion of the coast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, it's the state border. In simple terms, it's the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it existed during the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and during these critical years, and the situation is the same today. It was never touched, nor did any side challenge that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday we reached 3D01998.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We hadn't finished dealing with 996, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't finished with Franjo Tudjman's speech with the establishment of the Upper House of the Croatian Parliament. I was dealing with page 6 of Hrvatski Vojnik. I hadn't finished discussing that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's 3D31-0028, and in English it is 3D40-0805. Go ahead, General, please.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I finished saying what I wanted to, where Dr. Tudjman said that the Serbs would be guaranteed all civil rights and the right to local self-government according to the highest European standards and standards of the developing world, and that would be enshrined in the law. And here he talks about Croatia and the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he says that the causes of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina are quite clear; it's clear why they came about. And he says that Croatia -- that it's vitally important to Croatia for the war to end as soon as possible so that a political solution to the Bosnian and Herzegovinian crisis can be found, and that Croatia must remain vitally interested in resolving this problem. So we're not denying that Croatia is desirous of this. And then says why; because of the geo-political strategical links and interdependence between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then, B, because of the considerable portion of Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the number of inhabitants who have been there for centuries, for ages, and that it was a nation enjoying statehood. And, C, because of the effects of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the whole economy and the political circumstances in Croatia to such an extent that normalisation with respect to critical positions in the country could not be achieved until the Bosnian crisis is solved, which is of course logical, because without a solution in -- to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you can't resolve the UNPA zones because it's one army, one state, one battleground. And I, myself, was surprised by this pressure exerted by the Americans, that they wanted to -- well, I'd understand it if they wanted to divide it up, but had they positioned the army along our borders and then have someone solve the Bosnia-Herzegovina question. But the Serbs had taken all this [indicates], taken control of all these areas. And I didn't really understand how we were supposed to forget this fact. It was a political and military option. And, of course, the president knew exactly that unless you resolve the problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you couldn't resolve anything else. And that's what ultimately happened. It was only with the subsequent operations that took place with the international community's -- with Operation Storm, Flash and Storm, that the problem with Croatia was solved, the problem with the south was solved, and the problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina was solved, as it was solved. It goes on to say that the world, unfortunately, was not completely aware of the fact that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, all the problems that had been present in the former Yugoslavia had come to a head. Further on, he says that the time has come for the terrible war to stop, and he goes on saying what problems might arise if the war continues, because the Mujahedin has appeared. There are a lot of volunteers on the Serbian side from Greece, Eastern Orthodox Christians from Ukraine, from Moscow, and he says that the war could soon go beyond the regional borders. And then he speaks about the anti-fascist movement in Croatia for a simple reason. The reason being that for 30 or 40 years, propaganda messages had been coming from Belgrade and had been slowly accepted by the world. At the end of the day, Franjo Tudjman was also an Ustasha, he who had been a partisan from 4 years and a Yugoslav general until the 1960s. Bobetko too, who had been a partisan and a general between 1941 and 1945. I was an Ustasha. We were all Ustasha. And there were decades of lies that spread like propaganda, causing the feeling of nausea in all of us. We had to fight against those lies, although we were absolutely innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for the record -- excuse me, Mr. Kovacic. The page was indicated as the final three letters "805," but it must, I think, be 895.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 805, Your Honour. In English, in e-court, the last three digits are 805, and the page was also on the screen while it was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, I believe that yesterday you made a reference to the fact that the military prosecutor in Croatia was a Muslim, Colonel Baksic. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There's too much noise in the courtroom. The interpreter did not hear the last part of what Mr. Kovacic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The last couple of exchanges between Mr. Kovacic and the general have not be picked up by the English translation booth. They're saying there's too much background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, when you turn over the pages, try to be more silent, because it gives a lot of background noise to the booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just for my learned friend's information, I just asked General Praljak whether he wanted to continue talking about the military prosecutor, Colonel Baksic, which would be in the following article, and he was mentioned yesterday only in passing. The general said, No, and we are skipping that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, you said -- you said that -- we can also skip 3D1998.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe we should show two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then go on.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one is the Easter greetings to the supreme commander. Can you please produce what I wrote on the 27th of March to the HVO in Usora?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This one has been translated, and in Croatian e-court, it is 40892, and its translation -- I apologise. It is 3D40-892 in English, and in Croatian it is 3D31-0038. Go on, General. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usora, of course, is in Central Bosnia. I can't find it on the map at the moment. However, and for their own reasons, which I don't want to address, they wrote to Dr. Tudjman to inform him that they had broken off the Czech [as interpreted] offensive. They write that they had fired 20.000 different projectiles on them, that they had attacked with 34 tanks, and so on and so forth. However, it also says here that they did all that because of their heart and with the Muslim help. The offensive was quashed. They had 19 dead Muslim and Croat soldiers. And together with the civilians, there were a total of 162 wounded. And they also say in this letter that -- a reference is made to the Muslim province. And here you see the Vance-Owen Plan on cantonisation had already been signed and also ended up in the canton, and I'm imploring with everybody because this is being erroneously treated. A reference is made here to the Croatian provinces as the provinces which should only have Croatia population, but this is not right. This is the Vance-Owen Plan, and in order to make things simpler people said -- like here, they say that they remain in the Muslim province. By the same token, Croatian Muslims were also mentioned. There were no Muslim or Croatian provinces. For example, there should have been, allegedly, more Croats in Croat provinces. They were to be called Croatian provinces, but that has nothing to do with the interpretations according to which those provinces were to be pure. Muslim provinces, likewise, did not have to be pure. Muslims and Croats in Usora fought together against the Chetniks, as they described it in the letter. And they say president, that's how they address him, although he's not the president, still they address him as President Tudjman. And they are hoping that they would be part of an administrative unity because there were a lot of [indiscernible]. Of course, this is about Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are not talking about seceding, about being defending from -- defended from somebody. Mate Boban and Franjo Tudjman signed the Vance-Owen Plan, and this should have been implemented. The Serbs never signed it. Mr. Izetbegovic, after having signed it, as was his custom, gave up on it. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next article in the same --

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, skip that, forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we've skipped it.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment. Hold on, hold on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Seks?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we're not going to do Seks, no. No. No Seks, forget Seks, nothing important about Seks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the next "Hrvatski Vojnik" --

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we're moving to "We'll Build Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, can you give me the number?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If there is a pause, could we be told where Usora is? The Google map does not know a place called Usora.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usora is too small. I beg your pardon, begging your pardon? Pardon? I know, I know, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's right next to Doboj, Your Honour. That's where, I believe, the Vice-President Zubak was from, Usora. I believe it's now part of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see it. My eyesight is not that good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, "We Will Build Croatia," that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's in the same one, 3D01998, a long article, an interview with --

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an interview, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, it's not an interview. This is a speech delivered by President Tudjman. The Croatian e-court is 3D31-0044, and in English it is 3D40-0895 through to 0903. General, as you go through the subtitles, could you please stop and give me time to refer everybody to the Croatian and English pages in e-court.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I'll do that. This is what, in Croatian, is called the state of the union address. That's what it would be in America. Of course, we have a different name in Croatia for that. This is a most fundamental address by the president to the overall population of Croatia about the basic principles of the state policy in all the spheres of life, including wartimes and what is being attempted; culture, economy, and other things. So this is an equivalent of the state of the union address. I will start with the international circumstances in which we create an independent state. I'm doing this now, Your Honours, to show you how crystal clear it was to Franjo Tudjman, the president of the state, that he would not have been able to create a Croatian state if he had not understood all international historical circumstances that were at play and if he had not adjusted to those such circumstances. He was a historian and a statesman who knew so much. He knew so well what was going on, on the international scene, what kind of policies were in play. And here this is explained very thoroughly and in great detail. For one to expect that Franjo Tudjman would try to do something covertly with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina is completely beyond comprehension. Let's take things at a time. He says, and I'm going to give you the basic ideas, because it would take me too long to read everything, Your Honours, he says that the international order was against the creation of new independent states, that that order as regards Yugoslavia was based on the results and the outcomes of the First World War, which was the Versailles [Realtime transcript read in error "Warsaw"] agreement on the creation of a new Yugoslavia. He also says here that the establishment of new states were opposed by the states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I would only like to say that there is a mistake in the translation and the transcript, that when you spoke about the outcomes of the First World War, which, as you say, "which was the Warsaw agreement," of course you said Versailles agreement, so the "Warsaw" should be replaced by "Versailles." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. He goes on to say that even those who wanted to preserve Yugoslavia were against the establishment of a new independent Croatia. He explains what reasons guided them to support the former Yugoslavia, and he also says that the relationships in the former Yugoslavia were not favourable, that the most important representatives of Croatia in the institutions of Yugoslavia were also people who were not very much in favour of the creation of a new independent state of Croatia. And he goes on to say that everybody understood that Slovenia should let go if they so wanted, i.e., that Serbia was in favour of that, but that Bosnia and Herzegovina and other republics should remain in Yugoslavia, whereas Croatia would be given some confederal rights. Those were the proposals of asymmetrical federation. Those meetings ended with some preposterous solutions all to -- with aim to please Slobodan Milosevic. And the only thing that could please Slobodan Milosevic was a Greater Serbia. Then he goes on to say under 5 that Croatia was in a position where it was -- imposed the legacy of the independent state of Croatia, the historical independent state of Croatia, as a reason against the creation of a new independent state, and he says here that all that has to be born in mind because it is all still present, and that in all of that what one has to bear in mind is our overall international policy. Somebody who would think that they could go against all that would be nothing but a fool. There were some requests for speedy solutions in Croatia; of course there were. He goes on to say that there is a dissatisfaction in the Croatian people because of the fact that the Croatian administration had not been introduced in all of its areas, that this should have been done through our -- through force. And he also says -- and he's being asked why he's pursuing his policy, as he does, towards the solution of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is obvious that the international community has not been able to resolve that crisis through their pens [as interpreted] because they hesitated to resort to stronger political and military means. And now I quote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please quote the number of the English page on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because of the circumstances that prevailed at the time, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General Praljak. Perhaps there could be some assistance to the translators, because they're trying to keep up with you, General Praljak. You're reading quickly. The translators don't know the number of the page in English. So perhaps counsel could provide that information. I'm not conducting the direct. Otherwise, I would help you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. And I quote: "From the circumstances --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Where do you quote from, that was the question, and it is still an unanswered question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the same text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but the interpreters would like to know on which page. The pages have three columns. It is small print. Their task is difficult enough anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are now in the portion dealing with Croatia and the war in BH.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. "International circumstances in which we created an independent state." "International circumstances," that's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In English e-court, that's 3D40-0895, and then goes on to 896. Most of it is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you're not going to read this entire speech. It's extremely dense. Just please read the highlights only that support what you are submitting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was hoping I would do that, so that's what I'll do. From this text, which I hope will be admitted into evidence and will become part of the record, it is clear, crystal clear, that Franjo Tudjman understands all the elements working in the world politics, understands them with cold reason, and adapts his policies to those factors, aware of the fact that anything that might run contrary to the policy might lead to a collapse or might prevent the Croatian state from coming into being. And then he says that the policy he has pursued has been very careful, very cautious, clean, and that day after day he won over international players, acting in accordance with their demands, even though he was not always in accordance with them because those demands were often quite irrational and unreasonable. He goes on to say in the text that again the policy had to be prudent and that it led to the gradual understanding on the part of the international players and has resulted in the recognition of Croatia's independence and its admission into the membership of the United Nations. And then he says that one should not forget that Croatia on its route to independence was not armed; it had been disarmed, and that this state, such as it was, was able to set up a stable democracy, and that its constitution and other legal acts embodied all the civilizational achievements of the modern world, and so on. And then he goes on to say that we were recognised by 103 countries, that 75 countries, including the European community, have diplomatic relations with us, that we have good relations with the key great power in the world, the United States of America. And then he goes on to say that our legal system must guarantee all its citizens, in particular ethnic communities and national minorities, all their rights that have been achieved in modern humanity, that nothing will sway us from our way. And then he goes on to say that this has resulted in Croatia being able to sign the Vance Peace Plan, and that it is clear from what is going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what the Serb aggressor was ready to destroy in Croatia. And then he goes on to say, speaking about UNPROFOR, that UNPROFOR has fulfilled its tasks, and that there are some problems, but that they are being dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, now you've moved on to the second heading, "Problems with the protected areas and the UN." That would be 3D40-0897. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he speaks about UNPROFOR and how we managed to -- but before the war in BH, let me just remark, he says that he will pursue the same policy consistently and that citizens will be guaranteed all their civil and ethnic rights, including a right to self-government, in accordance with the highest civilizational achievements of Europe and the modern developed world. He speaks about a normalisation of the relations with Serbs under the auspices of the UN peacekeeping force. And then he says that Croatia is in favour of having free elections for local government in those areas, and proposes that the Croatian Parliament should make it possible for the representatives of Serbs from the two districts in which they have the majority, to be members of the Chamber of Counties in the Parliament, and also that the problem of Serb representatives in the Chamber of representatives should also be dealt with. So in the midst of this war, Franjo Tudjman says that for Kotor Glina, for the Glina and Knin districts, he offers the Serb representatives to have their own local self-government, their own police, as we will see later on, and to have their members in both chambers of the Croatian Parliament. And when he talks about the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. When he speaks about the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in English e-court, that would be 3D40-0898, and it spills over to page 0899. Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not repeat the three basic points, why he says that Croatia is interested in the actual solution. He says that some powers are getting involved in that war and that this might lead to an escalation; that the world has condemned the Serb aggression, but that there are some international factors that are afraid that there would be an Islamic state in the middle of Europe. And he says unfortunately those people who are not from the area, from the region, do not understand the problem, and he says that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina organised themselves to defend themselves against the aggression and was able to defend most of its area successfully, that the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina was saved in this manner, which was true. And then he goes on to say that under the auspices of the London, Geneva and New York Conferences, that the position taken by him as a matter of principle was always that any solution to the problem should be such that it would lead to a stable, long-lasting peace. And he says that Bosnia and Herzegovina can only survive as a state if it is made up of three constituent peoples who have equal rights, where they would have a certain degree of power in the areas where they have the majority because, as we will see further on, otherwise we would have the same thing that Bosnia-Herzegovina has seen for centuries now, that any solution imposed from the outside, the Turkish rule, the Austrian annexation, the Serb aspirations, any solution which would not be based on such principles would lead to a chaos in the country, as we are seeing now because the solution simply is not good, and it is all being postponed and the quantity of mistrust, not to say hatred, grows day by day. Well, I don't want to go into that. This is, in fact, an address which presents an overview, and I have to say that a man who understands and sees politics -- international politics in this way and the forces at play, and then to say that this man and this politics or the policy is plotting to annex parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, having carved it up, I think it's simply unreasonable. And we can go on. Let me just -- I'll tell you what I want --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. The next --

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'll skip the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll skip this one, to cut this short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving to this other document, I have a question coming from this speech which was delivered in front of the two chambers, a speech made by the president of Croatia, speaking before his citizens and the elected -- fellow citizens and elected officials. So he is there to talk about the policy that he's about to conduct. Now, given this, Mr. Praljak, I noted one thing. In this speech, President Tudjman addresses the problem of conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He says, Unfortunately in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are conflicts between the Croatian and the Muslim troops, and he adds "in some places." So he's not saying it's a widespread conflict. He's very careful and says that it only occurs in some places, and this is quite important. It's a president speaking to his people. He's not allowed to make any mistake, and what he says must actually reflect the truth or the reality. This is what he says, "in some places." And then it seems that he's going to give the reasons for all this. It seems that he says that it's the consequence of the Serbian aggression, that it also comes from the intentions and acts of irresponsible Muslim extremists. The analysis of the reasons of the conflict between Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina that he's actually carrying out, I would like to know whether the entire political class in Croatia at the time shared this opinion or whether here Tudjman is only expressing his personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I can't really give you an answer to that question because, of course, there were various texts and statements as to why the conflict broke out. There were those who blamed it only on Serbs, those who blamed it only on Muslims, and there were those who blamed only the HVO in Herceg-Bosna, because as President Tudjman once said, there would not have been any war in this area had Croatia agreed to remain in Yugoslavia. Well, it's very simple -- very simple to avoid war if you agree to remain a slave. And the same thing went for Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were no conflicts between Muslims and Croats here in Bihac [indicates]. There were no conflicts between Croats and Muslims in Posavina. There were no such conflicts here in the whole central area, Tuzla-Zenica, Zenica-Tuzla, and so on. There were conflicts in Konjic and in Central Bosnia, and then it spread. Of course, I share the position, and I will try to show what it was through the documents that I will call up in the course of my evidence, that several factors contributed to the conflict. One is the influx of a great number of refugees into that area, but this is my position, and I reached that position through conducting some analysis on my own. But the international community could not force the Serbs, who had taken large parts of the territory, to agree to any kind of logical peace, and then this part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina that Croats and Muslims were left with [indicates] simply made the negotiators, in particular I'm referring now to Mr. Izetbegovic and people who pursued his policy, because we will see that Mr. Izetbegovic was not really all that independent in pursuing this policy, to say, Okay, whatever we present to the international community as being under our control in the field, the international community is going to recognise it, because it recognised the Serb conquests, because it is not the purpose of the international community to get a just solution, but just to get peace at any cost. And born out of this kind of thinking, we had this kind of logic, that the BH Army should take Central Bosnia and should take, as it is stated by Sefer Halilovic explicitly, to get to its western borders and to get to Neum and to Ploce, and then to simply say to the international community, Well, we've dealt with the problem. Serbs have their own part; we've managed to capture our part of the territory. And I say to you, Your Honours, that they would have accepted that, because they accepted the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as Serbs did in the course of the war; 49 percent of an ethnically-cleansed state. Of course, this runs contrary to what I feel should be the moral fibre of the international politics, but there you have it. That's the real politic for you. And this is why this is Franjo Tudjman's position, but this is also the way that the entire government thought, including the parliament and everybody else who looked at things reasonably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, if you could please answer shortly, if you could give us shorter answers, you know, we could have more questions, that would be nice. I have one last question regarding this document, a question that I put through the -- by looking at the possibility that Mr. Tudjman might be playing a double game, which is the case alleged by the Prosecution. On page 3D40-0899 for the English version, the first column, the first paragraph of this first column on this page, he says, and I quote: "Croatia recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, and up until now it is the first and the only one who sent an ambassador to this country." Tudjman is thus saying that Croatia recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina first and sent an ambassador to this country. How can you interpret this, coming from Mr. Tudjman? Do you believe that in his mind, he is making a symbolic gesture, or is it a gesture that runs parallel to recognising a state, or is there something more, the fact that he wants to be number one -- the first one to send an ambassador, the first one to recognise the state? How can you analyse all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely in that way. If you want a country to remain integral, you're going to recognise it first, you're going to send an ambassador first, well, to Sarajevo, and it was Mr. Sancevic in this particular case. And Mr. Izetbegovic didn't want to take a plane and go to Sarajevo, or him to take a plane, and that would prevent some political gains, but not on the Croatian side. So let me repeat. Franjo Tudjman sent a prominent personage to spend a month in Bosnia-Herzegovina lobbying to have a referendum first because, Your Honours, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not prone to go to a referendum for retaining Bosnia-Herzegovina without a precise qualification of what kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina they were going to have, because the essence of the problem is not Bosnia-Herzegovina, as such, but what kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina it would be. I, as a citizen and Croat, what would I gain in that kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And it was expected that Mr. Izetbegovic would come out with a crystal clear -- and I had a long conversation with him in Mostar in October, that he would come out with a crystal-clear stand and say, I am offering to the Croats, Muslims, Bosniaks and Serbs, I'm offering this kind of system, internal system for Bosnia-Herzegovina, so let's fight for that social order. And I'm going to talk about this discussion I had with him in due course. So President Tudjman lobbied as much as he could to have this question of the referendum agreed to, and the Croats would not have agreed to that, and it was the Livanjski problem. I wouldn't have agree to that, either, because the crux of the matter was what kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina were we going to have, just as what is the position of France in Europe? What kind of country is Switzerland in Europe? So it wasn't a question of challenging Bosnia-Herzegovina as a country and state, per se, as such, not where the Croatian politics is concerned, but here we have a man who understands the significance of ambassadors and the United Nations and who is sending his envoy and all Islamic countries, Demirel's Turkey with whom /inaudible/ had exceptional contacts, they understood just how much Croatia had done for the Muslim population much better than the West understood this, because people came in from Iran, and Mr. Demirel, the president, was there several times, he set up a joint delegation with Mr. Tudjman to go to Mostar and try and find peace --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, just a minute. Your answers are very lengthy. Please try to cut it short. But you just said something that forces me to put a question to you. It's something new that I've just discovered. You just said that President Tudjman lobbied as much as he could to have the referendum, a referendum that could only lead to the existence of the Republic of Bosnia- Herzegovina. But logically, if President Tudjman intended to annex Herzegovina, shouldn't he then have lobbied with the Croats of Herzegovina or acted with them to tell them, you know, Say no in the referendum, vote no, because Croatia must be integrated? Wouldn't that be more logical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, what would have been more logical? He didn't even have to say, Don't vote. The Croats down there, without his influence, wouldn't have voted at all. In other words, the Badinter Commission would not be able to say that Bosnia-Herzegovina exists as a state, because two ethnic groups would be against, and quite simply we could have cut off that part without any problems, militarily and otherwise. We were far stronger than the BH Army. And in 1992 and when the war was going on down there, I, together with the HVO and Petkovic, we were able to take a chunk, just like the Serbs did; Uskoplje and Rama and Central Bosnia, and all the rest of it. But throughout that time, we assisted the BH Army and supplied it with weapons, so where's the logic there? You recognise a state and force or try and have the people recognise the state if you want to cut off a portion later on, and you send an envoy, you send an ambassador, you sign agreements. Well, that's precisely what I'm saying. It's quite unreasonable. I can't understand that. Nobody can understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have five minutes before the break. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps before we move on to the next document, General, while we're on the subject of responding to Judge Antonetti's question, you mentioned your personal meeting and conversation with Izetbegovic in October, and that was on page 34, line 5, of the transcript. Could you tell us what that year was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this brings us to document 3D0201 --

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only 0200, and I have a small part there that I would like to address. 3D02000, so three 0s, 2000, and it was an interviewed by today's Prime Minister Sanader. And at the time he was, I think, the deputy foreign minister, Dr. Ivo Sanader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. In Croatian, the page is --

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you. I'll tell you. It's page 11 of "Hrvatski Vojnik," and it just says: "Can we, within this context, stand up parallel to Serb diplomacy which has for years disseminated lies?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, it hasn't been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, on page 12, in the middle column, it says: "Dr. Sanader, you presented interesting views and the strengthening of cooperation between," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read it out. Dr. Sanader in that text says what kind of propaganda you have during a war, and everybody that has dealt with anything like this knows how many lies are disseminated, and I quote: "On Easter Monday, the 12th of April, 1993, the world news agencies broadcast a Serb lie to the effect that the conflicts between the Muslims and Croats in Travnik started by the nationalistic cry to genocide, appeal to genocide." And then this "fierce appeal" is in quotations: " ... none other," than once again in inverted commas, "the well known 'extremist,' the Croatian Defence Minister Gojko Susak. Allegedly, this piece of news was confirmed by two high-ranking officers of UNPROFOR. And on that same day, I reacted to this untruth, because I was present together with the other high-ranking officials of the HDZ at the great fair, Velesajam, where we held the main board meeting of the party. "Minister Susak," and you can see this from the papers, "was sitting in the first row at that meeting. Later on, Mr. Susak acknowledged that he'd never been to Travnik." Now, Your Honours, there you have it. This is one example, and this was mentioned for a long time later on, how war propaganda and lies were disseminated. And I think that some Prosecution documents mentioned that Gojko Susak delivered this speech in Travnik, and on the same day there's a photograph in the papers. Quite simply, propaganda and lies took on a great importance and were disseminated by and large all over, and unfortunately we did not manage to set up a television station and to be able to disseminate our own information and stand up to this misinformation that was broadcast to the world on a daily basis and caused major upsets and deviations of the truth. So that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, something was lost in translation. Can you just repeat your assertion. The sentence on page 37, line 17 and 18, wasn't quite clear. You said that Gojko Susak allegedly, according to certain sources, was in Travnik, whereas on that same day he was where, and where did his photograph appear?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at Velesajam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attending the main board meeting of the Croatian Democratic Community, and that on that day the papers published this, they published where he was. It came out in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that clarifies matters. Now let's take a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Please proceed, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, this 3D02001 and the next one, 2002, we're going to skip that to save a bit of time, and this brings us to 3D02003. And there's a long article there about the celebrations of the anti-fascist struggle and the 400 years of the battle of Sisak, and President Tudjman is speaking at length here about that. And you want to focus on certain issues. In Croatian e-court, it is 3D31-0076, and for the English it is 3D40-0929. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a two-fold meeting. On the 22nd of June, 1941, the 1st Partisan Detachment was established in Sisak of the anti-fascist council, and it was considered to be the first in Europe, setup in Europe, and also it was the 400th anniversary of the great battle of Sisak between the Croats and the Osmani Empire, the Ottoman Empire. And in history, it is considered that after that battle, which the Croats won, the burgeoning of the Ottoman Empire towards the West was stopped, and that was the beginning of the fall of the Ottoman Empire. And it is important to mention that all the members of the diplomatic corps were invited to attend the rally in Sisak and that there were two prominent anti-fascist fighters, partisans, Dr. Franjo Tudjman and Mr. Janko Bobetko, and they both delivered speeches. It's a long article, as I said, and following Judge Antonetti's instructions and guide-lines, I'd just like to emphasise that Franjo Tudjman was speaking about how the anti-fascist movement in Croatia was formed and how many partisans there were from the Croatian nation, without, of course, denying the part the Serbs played, the Serbs from Croatia. And proportionately, according to the number of inhabitants, he says - he won't omit to say that - there were more of them than there were Croats. And he goes on to say that the anti-fascist movement -- that there was a German detachment of the anti-fascist movement in Croatia, an Italian battalion, anti-fascist one, there was a Jewish battalion, a Czech brigade, a Muslim brigade. And further on he goes on to say that it was on the basis of this kind of anti-fascist movement in Croatia, contrary and opposing the Pavelic regime, that Croatia already at that time at the ZAVNOH and AVNOJ meetings, which were the constituent elements, that Croatia gained the constitutional right to its own republic, and he says that it was no province, it was not a province, as was claimed by some European statesmen, and that pursuant to the Constitution, the Croatian nation, the Croatian people, had the right to self-determination. Further on, he goes on to speak about how, through history, Serbian hegemony over the Croats developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. That is "Learn the lessons of history," is it? 3D40-0930 is the English e-court?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we're a long way from that. We're dealing with "Never Serbian hegemony in Croatia again," that title, and then we have "Croatia and the anti-fascist movement during the war."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and not overlap. It is impossible to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, it is at page 0 –“Croatia on the side of anti-fascism” is 3D40 -0931 in English and the subtitle "Never again a Serb hegemony in Croatia".

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not subtitles, they are headings of sections. Please don’t Mr. Kovacic. "Croatia on the side of anti-fascism during the Second World War," that's what I'd like to speak about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In English, it is 0931. That's the page. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reminds us here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wonder if you have listened to the interpreters, Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Praljak. They cannot follow you. Please, kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That was my mistake. I was trying to help out -- help the interpreters out by giving them the page numbers, so I -- but I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise to you too, Judge Prandler, and especially to the interpreters. Unfortunately, one's tongue and one's mind is linked; they are linked together. And even if I try to slow down my thoughts, unfortunately they tend to move rapidly, beyond my will, and that's where the problem comes. Anyway, he's reminding his friends in France here, and those who were not favorably disposed towards us for whatever reason, that the command of the resistance movement of Southern France was a Croat by the name of Ilic, who was given the rank of a French general and the highest French decoration, the Legion of Honour, and I think the Order of the War Cross as well. I think he was given that decoration too, and that the man afterwards became the husband of Zinka Kunc, who was a famous opera singer. She was an opera singer at the Metropolitan in New York. I've said all the rest of it about the constitutional decision and the right given to Croatia as an anti-fascist victor, et cetera. I'd like to move on now to another title which says "We want a political solution," and that is to be found on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In English, 3D40-0932 is where that part begins.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here he says what the Serbs want and how they want to achieve that. He refers again to the Knina Corps in Knin. He also offers a local self-government as something that they should get. He says that the military option is not what we want. And further on, he says that the normalisation of Croatian and Serb relationship is necessary for both Croatia and Serbia. And then he says that already some 20 years ago, at scientific meetings, he spoke -- he wrote that the time would come for the misfortunate Balkans to have reason prevail and that the Balkans will -- would become a new Scandinavia. This is something that Dr. Franjo Tudjman was dealing with before the war for some 20 years or so. Then he explains how the Finns, the Swedes, the Danes, and the Norwegians found a solution to their problem a long time before that. He also speaks about the Second World War and what a misfortunate event that was when the partisans waged a war against the Ustasha and the home guard, and the Catholics waged the war against the Orthodox, and that one should learn their lesson from history in order to avoid such happenings in the future. And further on, he speaks at great length how this would be in the best interests of Europe, how the Czechs and Slovaks managed to separate peacefully, as well as they did in the Soviet Union. I was following his political and scientific work, and I've always seen the same political theses. Now there is no Zagreb-Belgrade agreement of any sort, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now we're moving to 0933 in English e-court version.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: He again says that both -- that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina has come to an end through a political solution that will be satisfactory to all the three peoples there, because only that can be the foundation for a long-lasting and stable peace. He knew, as a historian, that all the former solutions for Bosnia-Herzegovina, starting with the Berlin Congress and others, were imposed on Bosnia and Herzegovina and always ended in a disaster. He goes on to provide a historical perspective and explain why things should be done the way they should be done, what happened throughout history if the political solutions were not good. And then again he speaks about Bosnia and Herzegovina and what happened there. He calls it a conflict, and he says that among the Muslims, as we all know, there appeared a thesis which they presented that they were not ready for the Serbs and that they, however, were ready for the Croats. He says that this is perilous, that this is tantamount to suicide. He also says that we have recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. He makes a reference and speaks at great length about refugees. He says that the Croatian population in Central Bosnia came under attack, that all Muslim politicians, soldiers, and all of them together, as we all know only too well and will be able to see from documents, are walking freely across Croatia as if they were in their own country, or even freer than in their own country. However, some of them provided statements to the press calling for the overthrow of the democratic government in Croatia. Finally, he concludes that it prompts one to ask oneself which God and Allah it was where they found such ideas and don’t they see where it is taking them. And again he says that the interests of the three peoples should be taken into account, a good solution. Always the same, more of the same, and always the same, and more of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we can move on to 3D02 -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Praljak, let us deal with this small topic which is, however, very important, the issue of the number of refugees. Mr. Tudjman says that there were half a million refugees that moved over to Croatia, 400.000 from Bosnia and Herzegovina. He says 400.000. That is a major number of people, and apparently he says that 272.000 people were Muslims. I'm trying to find some logic wherever I am. I try to understand. If the Republic of Croatia was in a state of mind that was connected with the Herceg-Bosna leaders, with a view to carrying out ethnic cleansing, why would it have harboured and welcomed 272.000 Muslims, whilst it could have been told to the Muslims that they were to go to areas that were controlled by the ABiH? Do you have an explanation for this, Mr. Praljak? How is it that 272.000 Muslims moved -- flowed to the Republic of Croatia? Why were they not directed to ABiH-controlled areas, rather than to the Republic of Croatia? Is there an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is, Your Honour. First of all, the number that is mentioned by Dr. Tudjman is probably just the current situation. There were a lot more refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and displaced persons, who either stayed in Croatia for a longer time or passed through it. First they would be received in Croatia, and then they would move on to some third countries that would receive them. Next, we saw the figure, and we heard it from Dr. Rebic, that the number was higher. Second of all, 70 percent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or maybe somewhat less, maybe 68 percent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs occupied in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The number of refugees from those territories was over a million, and some of the refugees stayed, and that constitutes the impaired ethnic balance or dis-balance. Some part of these people found accommodation in the territory under the control of the BH Army, and the HVO Mostar was swamped, Uskoplje was swamped, Central Bosnia was swamped with them. However, Your Honours, you can't -- the first excavators that were sent to amend the forest-path that led towards Rama, the well-known road of salvation, Mr. Stojic and I worked in 1992 and managed to convince some private persons who had excavators to give us the excavators and try and make a proper path, because before the vehicles would end up in the ditch. How could you not let people go? People just kept on coming and coming, and people kept on coming. You can't return those people and tell them, You can't go through. It never occurred to us to do that. We let through hundreds of thousands of people. The first station was in Posusje, where they would be fed and spend the night, and then they would be sent on their way. Transportation had to be arranged. Those vast amounts of people required resources and efforts that we just could not invest because we simply did not have the resources. For example, we would talk to three private owners of excavators who would then agree to do that, and then a British battalion came. And for their own reasons, they continued improving the road. There were wounded. There was no way one could send people back. You just could not leave them in the forest or on the road. When you have 15.000 people arriving in Rama, what can you do? It never occurred to us to send them back. These people were en route to Croatia, and Croatia went beyond all of their resources, filled up all the hotels along the Adriatic coast, every single house that could be used, and in doing that they had to make sure that these people should not be within the shelling range. For example, Sisak, Varazdin, Demistura, everything was full. It was bursting at the seams. There were Croats, from Bosnia, Muslims. Nobody was turned down, nobody was turned down ever, neither wounded nor a refugee. It never occurred to us to dwell upon what to do with them, where to send them. There was no ethnic cleanses. There was not even a remote thought to that effect. Those were people who were fleeing to save their lives, to save their hides, and they were received, they were accepted. And we worked day and night, as it were, under the conditions that prevailed at the time. And I believe that everybody knows only too well what the conditions were at the time, financial and all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm sure that you know the part where I led one of the operations, which was transferring people across the Neretva who had been expelled from Stolac, 15.000 people and 3.000 cars. I'll go back to that situation. We used a raft, a simple makeshift raft, to transport people and cars, some heavy lorries as well that we had managed to load, and they were all accommodated in Medjugorje, Citluk. Some were transferred on to Croatia, in the houses there. And now what was insulting at the time and still is insulting today, some of them who were not accommodated the first night. It was summer; they would remained outdoors; they would be given blankets, and then a European Monitor would come by and he would tell us, Look what you're doing. It was insulting then, and it is still insulting. If the conditions were not the way he thought they should be, as he had just arrived from Munich or Paris, or God knows where from, this was belittling the efforts that had been invested in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at 3D02004. This is an article entitled "Where there's no police, there's no life." This is an interview with the then minister of the interior of Croatia. I believe that you wanted to single out just one thing.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "A border without a barbed wire."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
