utterances.text: This is on Croatian e-court page 3D31-0091, and in English 0004 and on to 0005.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the first sentence here. He is asked, What state borders are you controlling? Answer, and he says, The state borders we are fully controlling today are the state borders with Hungary, Slovenia, Montenegro, and Italy on the sea, and one part of the state border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thus, the minister of the interior controls the state borders. And as for Bosnia and Herzegovina, he could not control the entire border because there were Serbs here [indicates], and he cannot control the narrow part in the west, because this is the free part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He cannot control this part here [indicates] because the Serb forces are across the border. And that would be all about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious that he's speaking about other states; Italy, Hungary, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia-Herzegovina is a different state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: 3D02005 is what we are skipping, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are skipping?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one article there. 006, that's "Hrvatski Vojnik" of the 10th of September, 1993, and here at page 4 -- or, rather, that's 3D31-0110. There is an article about a session of the National Security Council. It's called "For Herceg-Bosna in a united BiH." That's 3D40-0007, spilling over 0008 in the English version in e-court. Please go ahead, General. What did you want to say about it?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, a clear confirmation of the truth in this whole story, and that is that on that date the National Defence and Security Council in Croatia reiterates that as far as Croatia is concerned, that Bosnia and Herzegovina is an internationally-recognised member of the United Nations and that the proposal of the international community about the internal organisation of BiH as a union of three republics is accepted, and that Bosnia and Herzegovina -- that the war should be stopped, and that to the surprise of all international factors, Izetbegovic first agreed to it and then refused to sign it; that Croatia advocates Bosnia and Herzegovina as an internationally-recognised member of the United Nations; that it accepts the plan that was tabled; that it favours full compliance with the international law. And that's all I have to say. That's the end -- that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We will now skip 3D00208.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, General Praljak. Look at the photograph in this document, please. Is this the room in which the people who were received at the presidential palace were meeting? We'll soon come to the transcripts. You attended some of the meeting. Is this the room, the meeting room, the usual meeting room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That was the room where meetings were usually held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second question. We know that everything that was said was being recorded. Where were the microphones? Maybe you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the table, that's where the microphones were. Sorry? Well, I don't see it here, but I can see the little markers indicating who is to sit where, and it says here that a part of the session of the council, when Geneva Conference was discussed, was attended by Mate Boban, as a guest, and you can see he is third person on the right. There is Bobetko, Susak, Boban, with President Tudjman sitting at the head of the table, and to his right-hand side is Mesic. I said initially to the left, it's on the picture, but in real -- in actual fact, he was seated to his right. Then there's Seks, Mate Granic. And the picture is not all that clear, so I can't tell you who the others were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technical question. The National Security and Defence Council, when it came to meetings, was this one of the most secretive meetings? Is that the sort of meeting where you had the inner circle around the president of the republic? Was this the type of meetings that would gather the key actors, the key players, the closest people to the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was a decision on who comprised the National Defence and Security Council, and this decision clearly stipulates that. But one could say that this was the part of the military, police, the parliament, the speaker of the parliament. So key figures in all state institutions; the military, the parliament, the government, and the police, and the foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there were such meetings, would everybody agree or were there different opinions that might lead to the fact that what was said was being controlled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The meetings were very open in nature. There would be a topic on the agenda, and there was open debate about all those things. Whoever wanted to take the floor was free to do so and to present their opinions. Of course, there would be various questions, hypotheticals, If we do this or that, then what would happen? So it would be a typical debate of an analysis of the situation. So people did not go there to present their opinions. Often, people would say, Okay, if you say this, let me say the contrary thing to see whether your thesis holds water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the 10th of September, 1993. This document shows that a decision or an opinion is adopted by the people attending the meeting. It said that the Republic of Croatia continued to support the unity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this was said, could it be understood in two ways, a dual language, as it were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but whom were you to present this double language? The UN recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were ambassadors. Please believe me when I say this with utter sincerity. I simply cannot understand this argument, what this would mean. We say one thing, and then we'll do another. We are suppose to butt heads with the United Nations. Croatia recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina, sent its ambassador there, helped the refugees, helped arm the people, so I really can't understand. How could we do this in such an underhanded manner and take away parts of the country? So I'm asking this, okay, let's assume that we were lying, but please, can somebody tell me, what were we supposed to do in secret? Well, my brain simply ceases to operate there. I simply am not smart enough to understand this argument put forward by the Prosecution. I'm too stupid to understand it. I know the truth, because I was part of the whole chain of events right from the beginning, but I simply do not understand a single thing. And I'm saying this with utmost sincerity. There was nothing of the sort in thought or action. And we'll see what actions Croatia took to assist Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims, and the BH Army, and -- well, I simply cannot understand it, Your Honours. That's as much as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. This document reaffirms the fact that the Republic of Croatia also supports the Republic of Herceg-Bosna in the framework of the union of the three republics. It's written in black and white.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a proposal of the international community, and the international community tabled this proposal. This was not a proposal, as you will see from the documents that I will show you later, that Alija Izetbegovic's adviser -- well, we'll see those documents. Herceg-Bosna was a temporary, interim solution set up by a group of municipalities for the purposes of the defence. And as soon as the international community tabled its first proposal, that very moment, and I think that Mr. Karnavas presented all that, the moment they accepted the solution, everybody was ready to renounce Herceg-Bosna. So this headline here, I think it was the Vance-Stoltenberg -- or, rather, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, they tabled the plan, and Franjo Tudjman co-signed it on behalf of Croatia, and Boban immediately signed it on behalf of this Herceg-Bosna. So let me share a joke with you. There was a saying about Franjo Tudjman, Take away his pen, because he keeps signing everything, whatever the international community puts before him. There was -- there was some graffiti, Take away his pen. So there's really no behind-the-scenes games here. Well, he's not a fool. You have to read everything that he said. 103 countries recognised Croatia, and the United Nations, so now he's supposed to go and do something without getting the approval of the USA and France. Well, I really can't understand it. It must be that I'm stupid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, let me rephrase the question. The remaining two issues of "Hrvatski Vojnik," 3D224 and 228, do you perhaps want to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not "Hrvatski Vojnik." We'll deal with that later. It's a Muslim magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we won't be going into those two issues?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will need -- perhaps we can deal with just one minor matter. The day before yesterday, Your Honours, there was a discussion about the HV booklet and ID card, and General Praljak said that he had it in his possession, and he brought it with him. I suggested he should put it on the ELMO, and we have photocopies for everyone. So I would kindly ask the usher to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, could you please describe in your own words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we have a problem. We're running out of luck.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could perhaps you just show it to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that you look at the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you can show this another time, when it will be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can do that, but we just wanted to show that it didn't slip our mind, this whole discussion, and we wanted to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you had to provide us with the alternative before, and then this whole thing would start functioning earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is what we had, and it was introduced relatively late. This is the military ID card from the HVO. And this one, these two are from the Croatian Army. And here, let me show you -- sorry. Here, this is when I was a colonel, and this is when I became a major general [indicates], and you can see here it shows you that it was impossible to establish things properly, because I had to sign, myself, as the author, as the official, because there was nobody else to sign it in Sunja, when a signature was required. And here [indicates] this HVO ID card was issued on the 1st of May, 1992. And here [indicates] it's the military ID card from the BH Army. You can see I received it, and it was signed by Mr. Arif Pasalic. I think I got it when we went to Rama to try and calm the situation down. I think it was in late October 1992. His signature has faded, but you can see the stamp. But if you look with the magnifying-glass, you can see the signature of Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH Army in Mostar. I can show it to the Prosecution. If they look from this angle, they will see Arif Pasalic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the BH Army military ID card has an ID number, and we will be tendering it into evidence. We sought for that in our motion for late admission on the 65 ter list. And as regards those HV and HVO ID cards, we do not intend to tender them because it is a notorious fact that he was a member both of the HV and the HVO. But since this was a question pertaining to a soldier who was killed and who is mentioned in the Kordic/Cerkez judgement, so this man could be in the possession of only this ID card, and it doesn't contain any other details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's for sure. These are the only ID cards in existence, as -- and as you can see, I obviously fought, myself. It was a limited conflict between the HVO and the BH Army, or rather this conflict was very fierce, but it was limited to a short time-period and a small area, and in the end it died down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this completes our examination into this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Almost, almost. Mr. Kovacic, if I correctly recall and understood, we spoke not only of ID cards, but of a military booklet, and I just want to recall this. It appears that this booklet is not available. I am not saying that this is an essential piece of evidence at all, but together with this, it might have completed the display of the memorabilia of Mr. Praljak as a military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, a military booklet was introduced at a very late stage, after the first group of people who had been drafted, who actually did their regular national service, and this military booklet is never given to soldiers. It is kept in the Secretariat of Defence, in its files. It's the same thing with the work record booklet in Croatia. Nobody has it on them, rather it is kept –- they –- the booklets are not given to soldiers - the soldiers did not have them. They are kept in the filing cabinets of the secretariats of defence, the relevant secretariats of defence that were entitled to do draft people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me perhaps just explain my question, because my booklet, my military booklet, I have it at home, and all my services are listed and promotions and so on. That's why I thought it might be the same, and, of course, one always learns. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, yourself, did you have a military booklet? Was a military booklet made for you, kept at the Secretariat of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, my military booklet -- I received a military booklet two days before I left the Croatian Army in 1995, when I was going to report to the Secretariat in Tresnjevka municipality which is where I was in Zagreb, then they wrote out this booklet; they wrote in the entries, and said I was unfit for the army. Because from my JNA files they copied out what it said, then there was a commission decision proclaiming me unfit for military service in the JNA. Well, it made me laugh. I didn't mind what it said. Anyway, the booklet remained there, and that's where it is to this day. And until the age of 65 I am considered as being of military age, I could still be called up, but two days before I left the Croatian Army is when the booklet was made and issued. When I went to report there, that's when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But where is this booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Secretariat for National Defence of Tresnjevka municipality in Zagreb. Tresnjevka is a part of Zagreb; it's a municipality, one of the communes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking this question, because I would like to be sure that in this military booklet, there is only mention of unfit for military service. I would like to know, however, whether there aren't any other mentions of your various postings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The duties are certainly not stipulated in that booklet, no assignments, because I leafed through it, and I changed 15 or 17 duties during that period of time, not only in the army but other duties, and nobody knew about them to be able to record them and enter them. And I don't think anybody is interested in doing that today, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't wish to testify, but the general mentioned just one of the Zagreb municipalities. I come from a completely different part, and my booklet doesn't exist. I went to fetch it, and it's disappeared, because the former Secretariat of the SFRY probably didn't do their job properly and it got lost somewhere. But I don't think that's important anymore. My colleague, Ms. Nika Pinter, would like to carry on with the next chapter. We just need two minutes to confer. I don't think we need have a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: As far as the examination-in-chief is concerned, I think we should complete the topic of the presence of the Croatian Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina that we were discussing. So I'd like to ask you to open document P00153, please. It's a document which is in an exhibit already, and I'd like to ask you first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Pinter, you see behind us that we have a mountain of folders. Could you assist us in getting the right one, please. I see now that ours looks the same as yours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's the same, and I will give notice in advance in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I wanted to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Pinter adjust her microphone, please, and speak into it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is a document issued by Petar Stipetic, and it is instructions to a major, Mustafa Porobic, and other officers, P00153.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the truth is -- well, the deputy chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, Major General Petar Stipetic, says that at the request of the chief inspector of defence and general -- the highest-ranking general, should resolve sending part of the officers and soldiers of the Croatian Army from the operative zone of Rijeka, mainly Croats and Muslims, ready to go as volunteers to BiH to help the struggle of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that this had been accepted by the top military -- top-ranking military authorities. And this meant 300 to 400 soldiers and officers. And I know for sure that there were more than 300 Muslims and that they were led by Major Mustafa Porobic, and that they were going with full military equipment, weaponry and ammunition, and that what we repeated here 100 times is that they would retain their rights of BH soldiers -- the rights of HV soldiers and their monthly salaries. And the important thing is that they cannot wear HV insignia on their uniforms, nor can they hold other documents used by members of the HV, the Croatian Army, because that was prohibited. Now, of course, whether orders are carried out, you have a human being in between the orders that are to be carried out, so there are people who retain their insignia, did not take their HV insignia off, and then somebody sees them there, and then they say, Here we have a member of the Croatian Army fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That wasn't true. It was exactly as it is set out here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So they retained all the rights that soldiers of the HV had; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now look at 3D00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Praljak, you also made a normative statement. You said that wearing the insignia of HV would have been illegal. Can you explain why you say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say "illegal." That's a wrong interpretation. The order -- a lack of respect for the order. He said that the order was clear -- I said that the order was clear, and to respect an a order, in well-regulated armies and not national uprisings, because this was a popular uprising than anything else at that time, and of course some people wouldn't obey orders. And if they didn't obey orders, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You do not write this in every order that you give, of course. Nevertheless, you say it is prohibited. Why was it prohibited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because when they went over there, they weren't the Croatian Army; they were volunteers going to defend their homes. We didn't want the Croatian Army to go there, but we couldn't prevent individuals from going to help out their families if their parents were being killed over there. So who's going to listen to those orders? I would be the first not to listen to them, and I didn't listen to them. So you can't say, Judge Trechsel, Let them kill you over there because we have rules and regulations. If those are the rules and regulations, then I, for one, violate them. But Croatia said -- Croatia's stand was, You're not going there as Croatian soldiers, as members of the HV. You can go over there of your own free will, you can stand up to the enemy, your salary will be retained, and that's as clear as day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this you have told us many times. I do not say things. I ask questions. There's a big difference. And I asked the question because there could be another interpretation; namely, that Croatia did not want it to be known by people from other sides that they were sending their troops. You are saying, I suppose, and it may be something of a legal question, you are saying that this is completely wrong. There is no question of any wish of Croatia to hide the fact that soldiers, under the command of a major, whose name is given in the paper, are sent into Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Judge Trechsel. Just assume that you came to defend Croatia from Switzerland, for example, and then somebody happened to attack Switzerland, and then somebody says to you, You can't go to Switzerland. It was an attack by the Serbs against the non-Serbs. And I say that we never stated publicly that Croatia wanted to help the Muslims and Croa –- the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that didn't mean that we were sending our army, but that we were allowing volunteers to go and defend their homes and thresholds. And I always get a bit upset when this topic is raised, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I know it. Thank you. The comparison with Switzerland, I'm afraid, is not really very befitting for many reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ha, you could have come, you might have come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in this document there is a word, "volunteers." So as far as you know, were there Croats or Muslims in the Croatian Army who said, No, I have no intention and no desire to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Let's look at things military-wise, and, of course, I'm talking to a specialist here. Did things happen as follows: Say we have a given unit in the morning, when all the troops are collected and brought together. The colonel in charge of the unit says -- makes an announcement, says, We need 300 volunteers. Let's step forward, everyone. And the group steps forward, and the colonel says, Well, now I have got my 300 volunteers. Did it happen that way, or did the colonel tell the troops, You know what's happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina; we need volunteers; if you want to volunteer, raise your hand? So how did things happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of the two methods described by you. It was done in a third way, and that is that people on television or in the papers saw what was going on, and then they discussed it amongst themselves, for example. They would say, I'm from Doboj, I'm from Tuzla, I'm from some other place. And then they probably had their families there, their brother, their sister, their houses, and they would gather together and go to see their commander, and they said to him, Listen, this is the situation: I'd like to go and fight down there because I'm coming under threat. And then the person would give his permission. He would say, Okay, that's the position that's been adopted. You are discharged, although we'll keep a record of you as if you're still here. You'll be receiving your salary, and you can go down there. But you mustn't carry any HV insignia or HV IDs because you're going to a different country, to another state. And that's how I fled, that's how I went, in that same way. Who's going to stop me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Still on the same issue: These people were clearly put under a command here. How did they travel to Bosnia-Herzegovina, together under the command or individually? And if individually, how would they know where to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A broad spectrum there, Your Honours. This group around Porobic probably went in that way, in the group as it was, and then there were individual cases too. But, unfortunately, I didn't finish my answer. There were far more of those people who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina and didn't want to go down there and fight, and I was sorry to see that. They stayed on in Croatia and let whatever happen down there happen. So of the 13.000 who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Croatia Army, well, in the HVO I knew them all. If there was 600 -- I don't think there was 600. I can cut off my head if there were more than 600. Sometimes there would be individual groups. A group would arrive, and they weren't as they should be. There was a group called Jelen or "deer" in translation, and when I saw what they looked like and when I checked them out, I sent them packing. I told the military police to deal with them. I called their commander and I said, Listen here, mate, unless you leave this territory within the space of 12 hours, you'll end up in prison. And the military police gave instructions to deal with them. And there were people, of course, who came as volunteers, who were not in the Croatian Army. I mean, really, there was the chaos, on the one side, and then there were guide-lines and instructions that we gave, on the other. Now, when you have a situation like that, and men will be men, then various things happened. And if they were seen by observers, this would be wrongly interpreted. So they would go as this Porobic team went with him, and that was one of the groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And, Mr. Praljak, would you then consider those, that you threatened with arrest if they did not go, also as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were volunteers, but they were -- well, our services weren't such that I could check them out fully, but I didn't like the look of them, and I had my suspicions. Their conduct and behaviour was unacceptable. They sort of bragged and -- anyway, it was my decision, on the basis of my assessments, that a group like that couldn't be allowed to remain in the territory. You know, in conditions where you have limited access to information and you have three minutes or half a minute to make your decision, and you do make a decision, I made my decision, and I stand by that decision and those decisions, and I stand by them today. And I sent this lot packing, because I didn't think that they had come with honourable intentions. It was my own personal decision, and I stand by it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you mentioned 13.000 volunteers. This document shows that among the volunteers, there were Muslims. Out of the 13.000, approximately, sir, what would be the percentage of Muslims and of Croats, or possibly of Serbs? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there were any Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina. But in the Croatian Army there were a lot of Serbs in Sunja, where I was. There were 20 or so Serbs. The theatre of war there was very small, you know. I don't know how many Muslims and how many Croats there were, but I know that recently a list was compiled by the Muslim community in Croatia. They also established a memorial cemetery probably close to the mosque in Zagreb, and I believe that you could learn from them how many Muslims there were. But I'm sure that there was many more Croats than Muslims. I'm sure of that. I apologise, but there were also a lot of Muslims in the Croatian Army. The number was very high. I don't know how many there were. However, Your Honour -- please, please, Your Honour, please, Muslims who were in the Croatian Army from Bosnia-Herzegovina are one thing, and the other thing are Muslims who had resided and were citizens of the Republic of Croatia [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnia-Herzegovina"] we're talking about two separate groups here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's speak of the Muslims in --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting. I believe that we should correct a mistake in the transcript. On page 66, line 2, the second group of Muslims refers to the Muslims who reside and are citizens of the Republic of Croatia and not of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the first group are Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the second group are Muslims who are citizens of the Republic of Croatia. This is what General Praljak said, and it seemed very important to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I'd understood this. It's important, indeed, but I had understood. Let's speak of the Muslims in the group of Mustafa Porobic. They left in April 1992 or May 1992, they left for Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as you know, among those volunteers, these are HV volunteers, there were Muslims. Were there among them people who joined later on, who later joined the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I'm sure of that. Immediately upon arriving there, they joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They had to join an army. Some joined the HVO, and the others joined the BiH Army, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give short answers, because then I can follow up with very important topics, because you've just said something that is relevant. When the volunteers would leave for Bosnia and Herzegovina, would they be forced to join the HVO units, or were they free to join an HVO unit or an ABiH unit? Did they do whatever pleased them, or were they told, You've got to remove the HV insignia, but you have to join an HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. When they arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they could choose whether they were willing to join the BiH Army or the HVO. The group in question, as far as I know, and I know it very well, joined the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this group that we have here, that one joined the ABiH, and what did the Croats do who were with them? Did they also join the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. I don't know what happened. I believe -- I know that there were over 300 Muslims in this group and that they went to Central Bosnia and joined the BiH Army there somewhere. I don't know whether all the Croats joined somebody else or whether they were scattered all over the place. I believe that not only -- not even the whole group of Muslims joined one unit of the BiH Army. They actually went to their own villages and joined the army there. They went in the direction of the villages from which they hailed. They did not go there as a unit which placed itself at the disposal of the BiH Army. They scattered all over the territory under the BiH Army and the HVO, depending on their place of birth and depending on what they believed should be defended by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the level of the command, high-ranking military authorities, as is, by the way, shown by the document, because it says that the departure was accepted by high-ranking military authorities or top-ranking military authorities, had it been envisioned that the soldiers - these are Muslim soldiers - would go to the ABiH and might possibly return their -- or turn their weapons against the HVO Croats? Was that sort of situation envisioned, or was everybody innocent, candid, and they failed to assess the possible consequences of the action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment on that date, Stipetic and Spegelj could not think that the BiH Army would conflict with the HVO. There was no way for them to think that. I was one of the rare people who knew about the different interpretations of the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina which existed on the part of Alija Izetbegovic, on the one hand, and the Croats, on the other hand, and that this could lead to a conflict. I knew it very early on. I knew that while we were defending ourselves from the Serbs, we would be united. But when that was no longer in place, due to the different political positions with regard to the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there would be political conflicts. But the people that you mentioned certainly didn't know that. They thought that the Serbs were the enemy, the two other peoples were defending themselves, and they could not envisage any problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I would just like to say that on page 64 - maybe my learned friend Pinter could take Mr. Praljak to that - on lines between 6 and 9 there is something that is not clear. When he was talking about the unit called Jeleni, I thought that he had called the commander of the Jeleni group and told him that they had 12 hours to leave the territory, but it is not clear whom he called, whether he called the commander of the police or the commander of the Jeleni group. That's one thing. And the second thing is that the military police had been given instruction to deal with Jeleni, whereas it was recorded that the military police provided instructions for somebody to deal with the Jeleni. I believe that these are major errors in the transcripts which can be clarified in two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you heard that?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to the commander of the Jeleni unit and told him that he had to leave. I asked -- I demanded that Valentin Coric, the chief of the military police, to remove the unit Jeleni from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, following up on Judge Antonetti's question --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. This last statement by the general about his communication with Mr. Coric, could we get the time-frame in which that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, August or September, thereabouts. There is a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we are still talking about P00153. In the first paragraph of the document dated April 9, 1992, it says why the volunteers could be sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the purpose of their sending.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to help the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina in their fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now let's move on to document 3D00443. The date is 8 April, one day prior to the previous document. This document was issued by General Major Petar Stipetic. It was sent to the Operation Zone Split. The document speaks about the position of the Croatian Army, vis-a-vis the departure of the Croatian Army outside the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just repetition.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a repetition of what was said previously, that they can't bear the insignia. An attack had already been underway in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And why is there always a reference here to Rijeka and Split? There were a lot of people there from Bosnia-Herzegovina who worked in ship-building yards, who were welders and so on and so forth. And when the war started, they joined the Croatian Army. And at that moment somebody was destroying their homes, and they wanted to go there and fight the Croatian political and military authorities, because this is not happening without the political decision. Stipetic or I could not do it without ever having consulted with Minister Susak and Franjo Tudjman, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All sorts of assistance is approved by this document.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: With this document and the previous one, I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to Exhibit 3D0029. I'm sure you will remember the document. This is the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the office of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, rather, in the Republic of Croatia, which sent this to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say the number. It is 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam Pinter, to interrupt you, but I would like to ask a question about the previous document, which was document 3D00443. You submitted it before. My question is the following, and, of course, I asked you the question from Mr. Praljak. The very first sentence of this message, or rather, kind of comment, in my view, it says, and I quote: "The formation systems of the Croatian Army are not valid outside of the territory of the Republic of Croatia." So I believe that it is an important sentence, because the formation systems of the army, meaning that the units, how they were organised, et cetera, are not valid outside, of course, Croatia, but why should it be included, I mean this comment, why should it be included in that very message or comment by the commanding officer, the Petar Stipetic, if those units were anyway volunteers who went to Bosnia-Herzegovina to help? But in that very sentence, I feel that that was a kind of very determined comment that they should not look like the regular units of the Croatian Army. So my question is if that particular sentence, and the whole text, as a matter of fact -- because, for example, the third sentence speaks about the following: That the men cannot carry the HV insignias or any of the documents which we already talked about before. So I would like to seek for further clarification on this very matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour Judge Prandler. This is really very important, the formation or the establishment system of a unit, a company, a battalion. And here General Stipetic says that you can't send an establishment system. You accept the volunteers, you give them what you will, and then they should go there and they should establish their units within the HVO and the BH Army. Namely, let me explain, there were occurrences, especially in Posavina that appeared as a problem, that a lot of people were in the Croatian Army look here from the defence, because they were from villages, they had salaries, and so on and so forth. And those same people, and especially those around Slavonski Brod, most of them in the unit, for example, were from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and maybe even their commander was from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then what happened, which we're going to see in the following document, what happened was that the commander would say, I order my men to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, maybe 70 or 80 percent of the unit who hailed from there, and 30 percent were their comrades, and he therefore asked for the whole unit to go there with or without insignia. This should not have been done. You will see later on that there is a suit raised, and there is a warning here, you can't send a single establishment unit of the Croatian Army; you can send volunteers who will then join the military forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but you can't send the whole unit. In the following text, I will explain that partially. Ms. Nika, maybe you can move on to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, General Praljak. The question put by my fellow Judge is a relevant one. And you admitted yourself that the sentence was important, so that's why I want to revisit it. It is said that the formation systems of the Croatian Army are not valid outside of the territory of the Republic of Croatia. This is the initial sentence in the text. Very well. In order to understand my question, let us take the example of the NATO forces currently stationed in Afghanistan. If you have British units that are incorporated in the NATO forces, then the NATO rules will apply. If you have French troops, then the NATO rules will apply, in principle. But here, don't we have the same principle? Is this not to recall the military in the Croatian Army that from then on, because they are volunteers and they're going to go somewhere else, the Croatian Army rules do not apply, but probably other rules and operation that they have to comply with? Is this, to confirm a principle, a principle with consequences; namely, that there is no more control? What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know there is a provision in the Constitution, that was passed in a non-military spirit, that a Croatian soldier, as a Croatian soldier, as part of the establishment of the Croatian Army, must not engage in fighting outside of the borders of the Republic of Croatia. It was a provision in the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, and Minister Susak, in his TV show, actually said this in public. However, second thing, at the time and at no point later -- Izetbegovic, up until 1995, refused to sign a military agreement, because NATO goes to places where they have agreements with the army -- with the government. In Afghanistan, NATO has an agreement with the government there, and then there are units of the Croatian, German, French Army, I don't know -- okay, maybe not French, but English Army which are all covered by that agreement, and this could not be done here. Some commanders, for some reasons, because his house is on fire there and he wants to take his whole unit there, drafted orders to that effect. One of those was the major general, and then Franjo Tudjman demanded that this whole thing be investigated and that he be prosecuted. It was crystal clear, and you will see from the document where Mr. Bozo Budimir, a major general, is being indicted because he issued an order to a unit to move into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was not allowed to do that. He could do one thing, go there, join the HVO or the BH Army, as we said, under two bases; first of all, because it is unconstitutional and, secondly, because there was no military agreement. The military agreement that existed later made it possible for the army to operate in the border areas. The Croatian Army was allowed, and that is why I found it strange that the Americans were complaining and telling the HVO to move out of these areas, because in accordance with the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement, in the border areas the Croatian Army could take part in the joint defence effort. But if the order came to pull them out, well, they were pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us wrap up this topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This I consider, as my colleagues do, a central issue, really. I have two questions still with regard to this document. The first is: I note that the second sentence is: "The departure of volunteers," and I stress, "organised in adequate units, is granted." So here, at least, we have not a source which would allow individuals, on their own volition, to go into Bosnia and Herzegovina and look around and see with whom they would like to fight. Is there something else, another order that provides for this, or legislation? And I'll put the other question afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you always have to draw this distinction in our parts between principle and what could be implemented and the extent to which things were violated. Here, General Stipetic talks about the gathering in the Imotski Sector and engagement in accordance with the plan of the group.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the accused please speak into the microphone. The interpreters cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the accused while he was not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time in that area, and partially in Posavina, one thing does not exclude the other. If groups are formed, send them there in accordance with the operational plan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we really cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the plans that you saw with General Tokic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You cannot be heard, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're hearing anyone say -- the interpreters say that they're not able to hear the general when he's not speaking into the microphone. Everything he's been saying at the map has not been recorded because they're not hearing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe he will need to repeat it. Repeat again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just a moment, General. Perhaps it would be much simpler if we could put the map into e-court, and then the general won't have to turn around. He will be facing the microphone. So could we please have 3D03545.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for it, Judge Trechsel, I can tell you it's not either units or individuals, it's both. So there were many more cases involving the individuals going there, but right at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak, I'm quite aware. You have said so before. But here we have a document, and the document only supports one part of it. My question was: Is there any other document or did not one take the law or the order very strictly? I don't think a map is needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge Trechsel, law was complied with most strictly. We tendered documents from Split, from the Muslim organisation there, that sent hundreds of people into Croatia based on the same principle, and this has been explained in detail. This document speaks only about one segment, and that is if there are volunteers, they would be mostly from -- well, I don't know, that they should be deployed from Imotski to defend Livno and to carry out the breakthrough, to stop the JNA and the Republika Srpska Army at the beginning of the war, in accordance with the maps and the intentions, as indicated and as I showed with General Cokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now we have the map here.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are the axes of the attack, as anticipated, where Croatia must not send its troops for the defence. Well, Mostar is here [indicates] and Imotski [indicates] is there. So Imotski-Mostar. So they say, If you have a unit, send it to Imotski, and accordance with the plan --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, no, we can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then if you can't see it, there's nothing to be done about it. But we don't really need the map. The map is not really necessary. It just complicates matters. At this point, Stipetic is saying that the volunteers from Croatia -- well, he probably had somebody. He says, Well, it is expected that personnel would come from other units of the HV. So it's personnel, not units. People. And then they have to be organised. And in this part -- the first part, where the defence had to be set up from Livno and that area, they had to be sent there to assist in the defence against this first assault. It is quite clear the Croatian Army is not allowed to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a second question, and it refers to the last two words, "they are to be engaged according to the plan of the operative group." Could you explain to the Chamber what it has to understand? What is this operative group that decides on where these volunteers are engaged? It obviously shows that they do not go where they think it would be nice, or fit, or where their mother lives, or something like that, but they are in the hands of an operative group which tells them where to go. That's what the text -- that's how I read this text. Maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are wrong, Your Honour. General Stipetic at that time doesn't really know what's going on down there. He is not familiar with it. He didn't go down there. And it is a typical response of a trained officer, who says, Well, probably there is an operative group, and then let's do it in accordance with the plan of the operative group. There was no operative group on the 8th of April. I arrived there on the 10th of April. General Petkovic came on the 14th, and then it was only later that he was appointed the chief of the Main Staff. What operative group? Well, I don't know whether it existed or didn't exist. Of course, there was the Operational Zone Split. But for any operative group to exist -- well, later on, at the time when I came there, and among other things according to -- it was under my demands for people to go there to prevent the attack that I was talking about, General Roso came to this area facing Livno, and then he was followed by General Gotovina. I was replaced by somebody else, and General Petkovic was down there at all times. So it's just a military term. He, as a trained soldier, as a trained officer, he said, Well, probably there must be some operative group. But there were no operative groups down there. There were operational zones where everyone -- and I will, in the course of my testimony, show to you what operational zone really was, in actual fact. It was just an uprising. It was just an insurgency on the part of the people, and it takes months and months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now 12.30. We need to have our second and last break. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at document 3D00453. This document has already been admitted into evidence. It's a document that you, yourself, signed, so could you please tell the Judges what this is all about and how this document came into being.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. This document was engendered by the problems that cropped up. At that time, Croatia, so from the 3rd of January --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's the 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying on the 3rd of January, Croatia signed the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, but then the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the great problem -- the general position taken by the politicians and by the army, the command of the Croatian Army, was clear as to who and how and in what way can go to Bosnia and Herzegovina. But soldiers are human beings, in particular in the kind of army that we had at the time, and those human beings act -- well, they have this burning problem. The Serbs were attacking fiercely. Just before Bosnian Posavina fell completely, there was fierce fighting there with a huge number of casualties, so there was fighting involving the HVO, with many Muslims in its ranks. It was a mixed army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please face the microphone.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people who were in this operational zone of the Croatian Army [indicates], among those soldiers serving in the Croatian Army there were many people who had joined the Croatian Army from Bosnian Posavina. I was there in early July 1992, and I know for a fact what it looked like. For instance, there was the 139th and 157th -- or 137th and 159th Brigade of the Croatian Army, with 70 percent of the personnel from Bosnian Posavina, and they did not want to cross the Sava River. I talked to them. Half of them wanted to cross, half of them didn't want to cross. The commanders demanded that they should cross, saying that that part -- that area had to be defended because it would render Croatia much more difficult to defend. Of course, this was not in accordance with the instructions. Of course, in this document they say clearly some are -- some members issued orders for the river to be crossed, in contrary to all the rules that were in place. And I say that military judicial organs would take appropriate action. We'll see what kind of action. Of course, I agreed, these are human beings, everything is on fire, there is a war going on. I can't explain this in simple terms, but I fully agree with the position that Croatia has its interests in Bosnian Posavina. It's the border area, there are many Croats living there at the time, and in any time. And we are aware of the fact that some other operational zones faced the same problem. But the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a foreign country. We do have our vested interests there, but it is a foreign country. And the defence minister confirmed that in a televised interview. So repressive measures should be taken. Of course, they're angry because people do not want to comply, they don't want to cross, some of them don't want to cross, invoking the Constitution and other legal documents. So what should I then propose, but to have a dialogue and to discuss this issue, the fact that Chetniks are going to destroy everything, that we would have a new Vukovar. Everything that we knew would happen, and that really happened, and that this should be resolved through dialogue, through providing explanations that this cannot simply be cut off, just like that. In the French Army, there would be an order, and the troops would obey. That's as simple as that. But here it wasn't as simple as that, because it was not the kind of army that France or England have. Those were soldiers of a different kind. Well, it's simply difficult to explain. It was a different kind of a war. People were all mixed together from various places, and this was the inevitable result. So I proposed that only volunteers could be sent, that questionnaires should be sent out, and perhaps solutions should be found whereby soldiers would be offered three- or six-month contracts, and then under that contract they would have the status of a professional soldier. But this is something that the Personnel Administration should deal with. So this was a very intense war. There was fighting all over Croatia, a great number of casualties in Slavonski Brod. More than 500 children were being killed. And a whole series of human interests were present there, and they were present in the army, and they were conflicting interests, because people had their families, people serving in the army. And, unfortunately, it couldn't be dealt with in the way in which it would have been dealt with in the US Army or in the French Army; this is how it should be done, and this is how it's going to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could we please look at 3D017 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in the last paragraph we see a reference to contracts, to a contract. So is it the three- to six-month contract signed with the Republic of Croatia, or is it concluded with the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, HVO, or ABiH? Who is the other party signing the contract? On the one hand, we've got the volunteer soldier. Fine. But who is the other party to the contract?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina -- not Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the HVO, or anybody else had a contract with the soldier; nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say Croatia. Fine, but then there's something I don't understand. Let's assume that we have a soldier from the Croatian Army. He's in Zagreb, stationed in a unit somewhere in Zagreb, and he's a volunteer. He gets his pay and says, I want to volunteer. Is this the moment where he will sign a new contract with the Republic of Croatia, even though he already is paid, he's already on the payroll? How does this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were contracts between soldiers and the Croatian Army about the professional status, only for guards brigades, not for the rest. In other words, while he was there, mobilised or whatever, he would receive a salary. As soon as, for some reason, he stepped down, he forfeited his salary. And here the proposal is to offer up a three-month contract to volunteers, because he could say, I want to go there, but as soon as I go, my family will be left without a livelihood. So I would like to go, but provide me with an agreement or contract of some kind; first of all, if I am killed, that they receive state benefits. So that would be a kind of contract for a three-month period or a six-month period, because people had to deal with questions of livelihood. But with Croatia, not with anybody else. They could just sign these contracts with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, this very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Perhaps this is an opportune moment, General, for us to go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I also have a question. I seem to understand, but I always stand to be corrected, that the war you were speaking about here was the Muslim and the Croats together against the Serbs. Now, there has been an allegation in the indictment of Croatian troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina fighting against the Muslims, and there the issue of international armed conflict arises. But does it arise in any way -- is there any problem if Croatia sends her troops, with the consent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight the common enemy, which then would be an international armed conflict that exists anyway between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, on one side, and the Serbs on the other side? If you could explain. I seem to sense that Mr. Karnavas would like to jump up and explain it all, but I must ask the witness, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to explain it. I'm a little bit puzzled, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm a little bit puzzled by the question, Your Honour, only on the sense -- I think it's a very good question. Don't get me wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You can expect that from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I can be surprising at times. But it does seem to -- you seem to be requesting a legal opinion at this point in time. Based on the question itself, one could interpret that question to be eliciting a legal opinion from a layperson. Now, I suspect, you know, the question, as you wish to put it, is whether it was his understanding, given that he's indicated that he studied some law, but otherwise it would appear that you're asking a question that is best put to an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You certainly have a point there, and it goes against my own attitude if I ask a legal question. Maybe I withdraw the question. But I want to correct the transcript on line 14, on page 84. What I was saying a bit jokingly is I was putting it to you that you did not expect me to ask a very good question, but that was meant as a joke, and it needs no further intervention. Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, just a minute. My fellow Judge is withdrawing this question, but I'd like to come back to it, because he said something very important, something that I had neglected to see up until now. We see this volunteer system, which you have described, and I'm sure that the Prosecutor and during the cross-examination will shed light on this and bring his own opinion to this. But my fellow Judge addressed a very important issue, I believe. There is a conflict going on against the Serbs, so could you tell us why it is that the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the framework of a partnership or cooperation, did not officially start fighting against the Serbs, but in an official manner and jointly, then the Croatian Army could have officially crossed the border in order to go help out, if I could say so, the ABiH in the struggle against the common enemy? Why was this not done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Mr. Alija Izetbegovic didn't agree to that. On the Croatian side, a proposal of that kind was put forward, it existed, because there was a joint enemy, a common foe with a clear-cut strategic goal, and we were to stand up to a common foe together, jointly. However, if, Your Honour, you go back to the facts and look at them - and I'm going to demonstrate that in due course - Alija Izetbegovic tried to reach a historical agreement with the Serbs, and by the village of Ravno he said, It's not our war, that a few days before Sarajevo - and I'm going to show documents to bear that out - was bombed, he said, There won't be a war because you need two to tango, two to enter into a war, and they weren't in favour of a war. So he claimed several times, and we saw a document to this effect, that the Yugoslav People's Army would ensure peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the gentleman whom I know, and I respect him on many counts, but quite simply either didn't want to understand, or couldn't understand or whatever, what it was all about. He thought that the war -- he would be able to avoid a war. And he refused to enter into an agreement of that kind, the kind that you have just mentioned, a military cooperation, right up until 1995. When he signed it in Split, it was only then, pursuant to that agreement, that it was possible for the Croatian forces, after Knin, to move to, say, Bihac and move on towards Banja Luka, and join up with the BH Army and the HVO to liberate this entire area. Unfortunately, he signed this in the summer of 1992. He only signed an agreement on borders, and we're dealing with borders here. That's what the agreement related to, and that is why all these different interpretations arose as to whether you could issue an order to cross the border for a 20 or 30 belt to refute the Serb artillery that was targeting Croatian towns, Slavonski Brod, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you're saying is important. He did not want the Republic of Croatia to officially enter into Bosnia-Herzegovina to help out. But he knew there were volunteers, so implicitly he accepted the fact that Croatia would help through these volunteers that were sent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Then, at that time, during that period, he already realised the mistakes that were made, and this is logical. He began taking in people from the Islamic world, because when he was placed in this situation, any aid he could get was of fateful importance to his people. Of course, the people who came in, for example, from the Islamic countries, and we refer to them later as the Mujahedin, it didn't say on their forehead what kind of people they were. He was facing a terrible defeat, so he took the hand offered to him. Now, what they did later on, we can't criticise that now, because it was -- he was catching at straws at that particular point in time. And at this time, Alija Izetbegovic from Zagreb, together with his whole entourage, arrived in Slavonski Brod and asked, because it was -- he was already on the brink of destruction, whether he could send an army from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that, of course, was completely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, each time you're answering, you're opening doors to new important issues. You say that he brought in the Mujahedins because he had no other way out, given the situation, which is what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If not, please tell us what you said, because this is what I thought I understood. I thought you said that given the situation -- so please tell us what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not accept the Mujahedin, but volunteers. He took in volunteers. Later on, it transpired that they came to fight for the Islamic cause and to disseminate Islamism. But, you see, when somebody is offering you a hand, you grab hold of that hand, and you don't know who the hand belongs to. It might belong to Hitler, but at that point in time you just see the hand being offered to you, the helping hand. So what I'm saying is that most probably Izetbegovic did not know what the Mujahedins would bring with them. He accepted assistance. He accepted everything from Croatia and from others too, because he was in this catastrophic situation, militarily speaking. The Serbs were about to take Sarajevo, and I don't know how Bosnia and Herzegovina would have survived had that happened, notwithstanding the international recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to discuss document 3D00299 now, please. I don't think you have it in your binder. It's already an exhibit. But when I put the document to you, I'd like to ask you how this was possible when I put it to you. Now, you can see the document on the screen in front of you. It is a letter sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. The date is the 4th of January, 1993. It is signed by Colonel Hasan Efendic, who was the secretary for military affairs, attached to the Office of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia. And in that letter, Colonel Hasan Efendic asks the Ministry of Defence permission for the purposes of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to engage officers of the Croatian Army; and they were Ismet Avdic, who was a colonel, Ahmet Puskar, who was a major and who was in Dubrovnik, engaged in the defence of Dubrovnik, and Dr. Sadik Rakanovic, who was also a colonel. Furthermore, in this request it says that the status of these officers would be resolved as had been the case thus far; that is to say, their status would be put on hold. They would enjoy all the benefits as officers of the Croatian Army. And once they had completed their assignment, to enable them to continue their engagement in the Croatian Army. I'd now like to ask you to explain to the Court how that was possible.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, it wasn't -- it wasn't that it was possible. That's how it was. And that's what I'm saying throughout. Bosnia-Herzegovina had its representative offices in Croatia. We see we had this military office in Croatia, and later on you'll be able to see that it had branch offices of the Main Staff of the BH Army for logistics in Zagreb, having been given permission from the Croatian government, of course. So it's all quite clear, it's crystal clear. If you look at the basic premise, they talked to these people, these people said, Yes, we're ready to go and help out, but hold our status on hold, keep our status on hold, because when we come back, we'll take it up again. And two days ago, when I was talking about Jasmin Jaganac [phoen], he was in the war, he was in Mostar, and he went back to the Croatian Army. That was a rule. Assistants of the Republic of Croatia took that form; they said, Volunteers, you can go, your status will be retained. If you're not killed, come back and you can take up your status. If you are killed, your family will enjoy all the benefits and rights befitting a Croatian soldier, just in the same way as if he had been killed in the defence of the Republic of Croatia. And that's what the situation was like throughout, in all its aspects.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And those three people were Bosniaks, were they, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Let's move on now, and I'd like to show a video. 3D03127 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, of course this document deserves our in-depth scrutiny. Obviously, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is asking for three officers of the Croatian Army to be assigned so that they can actually work within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They're doing this on January 4th, 1993. We were reading this document, I was listening to the question put to you by your counsel and your answer, and I could only make the connection with what happened in Prozor in October -- what had happened in Prozor a few weeks earlier in October/November. If the high authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina is sending this demand, even though they knew what had happened in Prozor, what could they infer as to what had happened in Prozor regarding this? It was just a skirmish, or was it an incident that was to be integrated within the plan? What can you say? We know that you were in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A local incident -- this was a local incident, and here, when I am going to talk about that, when I went there to calm the situation down there, and then I went on to go to Uskoplje, I had been asked to go there, and I can't really be sure whether -- or, actually, Mr. Izetbegovic was there during one of the requests. Franjo Tudjman was there both times, and they were imploring me, Praljak, go, please. At one of them, the president told me, Praljak, go there. We don't want a war with the Muslims. Please try and calm them down. It was a local incident. After that, I stayed in Central Bosnia for a long time, and in a month and a half, in the territory of Konjic, Rama, Uskoplje, Travnik, Novi Travnik, in the defence of Travnik from an onslaught of Serbs after the fall of Jajce, I managed to calm the situation down to a large extent. However, the fuel was rekindled. Things went step by step. The fire was rekindled. The negotiations went through. It was an organic development, and things went from bad to worse. And all the time up to the 30th of June, and even after Jajce, I'm going to show it crystally clear. In my engagement there was a will -- there was a desire and a hope that we would avoid a conflict, that we would not be attacked, and that was again a limited -- Croatia, not then, you will see later on when we come to that, in the summer of 1993, allowed the staff of the BiH Army to establish its logistics centres in Zagreb, Rijeka, and Split, to work in the territory of Croatia. We gave them everything, although the conflict in Central Bosnia and in Konjic had already been underway, there had been already initial conflicts with Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, just for record, when you said all that was up to the 30th June, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I apologise. We have to have a clear temporal framework. You continued talking about Jajce. That's why --

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. No, no, no, that's when the conflict was already clear. But even after that, the Republic of Croatia did not change anything with regard to the assistance to the BiH Army, nothing. It became a bit more difficult to implement and transport the weapons over there. However, nothing changed in the general approach to the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask the Court to produce video 3D03127. And, General, I'm going to ask you once the video is over, to provide your explanation, but let's first look at the video and listen to what it says. Can you tell us who --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is there an exhibit number for this, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 3D3127. It's already on the record. We seem to be having a problem with the technical issues. There's no sound. Unfortunately, we will not be able to run the video at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, while we are waiting to see what happened: You are familiar with this. This was a show “U krupnom planu” on the Croatian Television.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who were the guests on that show?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Gojko Susak that we see. Now, there was also General Lucic, there was myself, and a few other from the Personnel Administration who answered some other questions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there were people from Social Welfare as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the topic of your discussion on that show?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: All sorts of issues were on the table; the rights of the Croatian Army, looking after their welfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know that there was also a reference made to the departure of the Croatian soldiers to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
