utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a leading question. If we could just -- if we're going to listen to the video, that's fine. Otherwise, perhaps, we should just move on and come back to it, because it's not very helpful at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer seldom intervenes, but when he does so, it's always for a good point. Indeed, if you're going to run the soundtrack, no use in putting a question before, unless you give it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depends on the technical service, whether we're going to see it or not. It's not up to us. Unfortunately, we still don't have any sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for the sound to appear, just one question. When this show aired, do you remember, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: That aired either in July 1992 or maybe the beginning of August, somewhere around that time. I can't be really sure of the exact time, but I know that it was after my return from Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they don't have the transcript of the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There is also an explanation provided by the minister to explain --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should be said about this part is this: People ask why the Croatian Army does not intervene in Bosnia Posavina, knowing fully well that from Bosnia and Posavina, from the occupied part, the Serbs are pounding and killing people in the areas around the Croatian border. And Susak says, We're doing what we can, and we assist as much as we can. The second question was -- or the second part of his answer was this: Croatia is not in a war, Croatia has just signed a cease-fire. And there was also a question coming from a mother whether a soldier, a Croatian soldier who refuses to cross the border and go to Derventa, will be punished, and he says, No, and explains. President Franjo Tudjman, himself, and a few high-ranking officers spelled it out very clearly. Volunteers who hail from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also others who want to volunteer and go of their own will to fight against the enemy, who is common, Croatia had signed a cease-fire, but war did not end with that. They could go under the conditions as specified herein, and nothing clearer then could be said. This was the state policy, and the state policy also dictated the position of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the information for the Trial Chamber, the transcript in English of Minister Susak's answer bears the following number: 3D41-0682 and 3D41-0683.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I would now like to go on working, and I would like to ask you to tell us something about a document that you already mentioned. 3D00963 is its numbers -- number. And together with this document there is also 3D01719. The first document, 3D00963, is a decision by the president, Dr. Franjo Tudjman about the appointment of a commission that would investigate some of the actions and orders issued by General Major Bozo Budimir. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here, under item 1 of this request issued by the supreme commander, it says as follows: Why did the major general make a decision and issue an order to send the 57th Independent Battalion to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Bosnian Posavina? He never had such an authority from the Main Staff. There are some other things here, but I believe that this is one of the things -- one of the calls for an investigation of that case. This person was the commander of the operation zone in Sisak, and he was my commander when I was in Sunja. He is a wonderful man, a former officer of the JNA, but he was full of desire to fight. He wanted to fight the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska, and he breached a previous order. And he was not the only one. Let's be clear on that. There were a lot of such things going on in Bosnia Posavina, and things were dealt with in the way that they would be dealt with. He was called to task and processed, and the others were just called to their senses through a conversation telling them that they shouldn't do such things, but that they should follow a procedure. And this was probably the best way to proceed in such situations, and the principle had to be respected. However, when people are being killed, when people are dying, for example, when in a big town you have 28 killed children and in its broader surroundings some 500 dead civilians, all the commands, all the laws, assume a different perspective. The perspective changes quite a lot, as a matter of fact. Where there is death, where there is blood, dead children, all that creates in people -- an organised -- well-organised army would deal with those matters differently, but those were their next of kin, their closest family and relatives, and only human reactions could be expected. They did not follow any rules, but they were still human reactions. And rules did apply. We adhered to the rules, and whenever somebody broke a rule, there would be an investigation, even of an honest man like this person in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you please look at 3D01719. Now to round off this topic, this is a proposal to indict by the prosecutor of the Military Court, and I believe that this was taken even further.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This person willfully used HVO units, unbeknownst to the Main Staff of the HV. Posavina is not specifically mentioned, but I know that he did that. And I don't know how that all ended. I know that he was punished in one way or another. And I know that he was hurt by all the developments, because he also was a volunteer. He was in Sisak when I was in Sunja. He was a volunteer. He was a soldier. He knew exactly what discipline was, and everything else. But, you know, there's no single military where all the commanders obey all the commands. There is a misperception that a military is something like a firm mechanical mechanism. This is not true in any military. In America and France, when a war starts, when people start dying and bleeding, every military experiences lots of problems. I already shared with you one case that I know from history. General de Gaulle did not obey Eisenhower's words when he said that his troops would not enter Paris first. De Gaulle did not like that, and he sent the 3rd Army of General Leclerc to enter Paris first, out of spite. Well, you know, things are not as simple as they seem on the face of them. It's not like a laboratory experiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just for the record, on page 97, line 22, the number of the document that the general has just referred to is 3D01719. We've wrapped up this topic, as far as our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like this 3D1719?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, we did that.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's the motion to indict.

utterances.speaker: Slobodan Praljak [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's Stipetic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We've dealt with that through "Hrvatski Vojnik," right at the beginning, so we don't want to repeat ourselves. Our next topic is the assistance of the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am now in the hands of the Trial Chamber. Should we embark on this new topic, or should we adjourn now and begin tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but for a few minutes, the moment has come to adjourn. It might be better to start with a new topic tomorrow. If you don't mind, General, we could move on to a new topic tomorrow. Is that okay? Very well. As you know, we'll be sitting in the morning tomorrow. The hearing will start at 9.00. Thank you. The hearing stands adjourned. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
